strategies.intent: replace cuBLAS GEMM plus separate post-op path with a cuBLASLt matmul-centered pipeline that fuses whatever is legal per mode
strategies.summary: The current champion leaves the hot kernel as `ampere_sgemm_128x128_tn`, and NCU shows ~72% SM throughput but only ~33% active warps with 118 registers/thread, so the main win is not another tiny post-op kernel; it is reducing launches around the GEMM and moving eval-mode post-ops into a GEMM epilogue or folded parameters. In training, keep GEMM as the producer and fuse only the remaining normalization/activation work as tightly as correctness allows.
implementation_hints: Add a backend path that distinguishes BatchNorm training vs eval explicitly at the forward call site.

For eval mode, fold BatchNorm into linear weights/bias using running_mean/running_var/gamma/beta, then dispatch a cuBLASLt matmul with fused bias/activation epilogue where possible; ReLU is easier than GELU, so prefer the strongest supported epilogue combination and avoid extra tensor materialization.
For training mode, keep the GEMM library call but avoid re-reading/writing intermediates more than once after GEMM; the fused post-op path should consume the GEMM output immediately.
Reuse persistent cuBLASLt descriptors/workspace from helper anchors instead of rebuilding them every call.
strategies.expected_gain: medium to high in eval-heavy paths; low to medium in training if launch overhead and one intermediate write can be removed
risk_notes: BatchNorm folding is only valid in eval/inference mode using running statistics, not training statistics.
cuBLASLt epilogue support is version- and dtype-dependent; unsupported combinations can silently force fallback planning.
Must preserve output shape/dtype and exact BatchNorm epsilon/affine semantics.
memory_methods: parameter folding to eliminate BN tensor traffic in eval
epilogue fusion to avoid separate activation output buffers
forbidden_patterns: do not fold BatchNorm during training
do not change normalized axis from feature dimension
do not approximate BN with per-tile statistics

review_notes.openai-compatible: Strongest risk-adjusted option. Folding BatchNorm into weights/bias in eval is standard and high-value, and cuBLASLt epilogues can remove extra launches/materialization without replacing the GEMM. Clear mode split respects training-vs-eval semantics, with main risks limited to epilogue support and exact epsilon/affine handling.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Best risk-adjusted option. Parameter folding for eval mode is a proven, low-overhead technique that eliminates BN tensor traffic entirely. cuBLASLt epilogue fusion for bias+ReLU is mature on Ampere; GELU epilogue support exists but is version-dependent. Training mode is harder but the eval path alone justifies the work. Main risk is cuBLASLt planner falling back silently on unsupported epilogue combos â easily mitigated by an explicit capability check.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using cuBLASLt and folding BatchNorm into weights (if applicable for eval mode) is a highly effective strategy, though it requires careful handling of training vs. eval modes.

strategies.intent: turn training-mode BatchNorm into a two-stage GEMM-adjacent reduction pipeline instead of a feature-per-block scalar kernel
strategies.summary: The existing fused BN+GELU+ReLU kernel likely underperforms because each block owns one feature column and streams the full batch, which is reduction-heavy and poorly matched to the large 16384x4096 activation. A better CUDA training path is a dedicated statistics kernel with row/column tiling and vectorized loads, followed by a normalization+activation kernel, while still keeping GEMM on cuBLAS.
implementation_hints: Split training BatchNorm into a first kernel that computes exact per-feature mean and variance over the batch using tiled reductions across the 2D GEMM output, then a second kernel that applies affine + GELU + ReLU in one pass.
Map blocks over 2D tiles of the activation rather than one block per feature; accumulate partial sums/sumsq per feature tile in shared memory and reduce across warps efficiently.
Vectorize global memory accesses along contiguous feature dimension when alignment permits, and keep running-stat updates outside the hot elementwise pass.
Use the fused activation kernel only after exact statistics are finalized to preserve BatchNorm semantics.
strategies.expected_gain: medium for training workloads where BN statistics cost is nontrivial relative to GEMM tail work
risk_notes: Requires careful reduction ordering to remain numerically stable and exactly preserve BatchNorm axes.
Extra staging for partial reductions can backfire if feature-tile sizing is poor.
May still lose to native PyTorch kernels if synchronization or atomics are overused.
forbidden_patterns: do not update running stats from per-tile approximations
do not emit separate GELU and ReLU kernels after normalization
do not keep one-block-per-feature mapping as the main training design

review_notes.openai-compatible: Good training-path strategy. Keeping GEMM on cuBLAS while redesigning BatchNorm training into exact tiled stats plus fused apply is much more realistic than a fully custom GEMM. It aligns with the normalization constraints, though reduction ordering, staging, and synchronization still need careful numerical validation.
review_notes.claude-compatible: A well-targeted training-mode improvement. Replacing the one-block-per-feature design with 2D tiled reductions addresses a real structural inefficiency in the statistics kernel. Medium complexity, and the expected gain is genuinely bounded by how much BN statistics cost relative to GEMM tail work. Partial-reduction ordering and atomics need care to stay numerically stable and not degrade occupancy.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Keeping cuBLAS for the GEMM and optimizing the BatchNorm into a fast two-stage reduction and apply pipeline is the most realistic and effective approach for training mode.

strategies.intent: reduce occupancy pressure in the custom CUDA post-op by redesigning for warp-specialized vectorized elementwise throughput
strategies.summary: NCU reports register-limited occupancy (`launch__registers_per_thread=118`, register occupancy limit active, only ~33% active warps), so even if post-ops are not dominant, any custom CUDA path should avoid heavy scalar control/reduction state. A leaner kernel can improve overlap and reduce the chance that the fused path is slower than PyTorch primitives.
implementation_hints: Separate reduction state from elementwise state so the activation-application kernel uses far fewer live values and lower register pressure.
Prefer warp-specialized or CTA-specialized roles instead of every thread carrying both reduction and activation temporaries.
Use vectorized `float2`/`float4` loads and stores on contiguous feature slices for the apply kernel, with tail handling kept simple.
If GELU remains fused, choose the fastest acceptable formulation consistently and avoid extra temporary buffers or branchy mode handling inside the inner loop.
strategies.expected_gain: low to medium; mostly improves the viability of the custom path rather than changing the global bottleneck alone
risk_notes: Because GEMM remains dominant, this alone may not move end-to-end runtime much.
Aggressive vectorization depends on alignment/contiguity guarantees at the call site.
Changing GELU approximation details can alter correctness if not matched to the framework path.
memory_methods: reduction/apply kernel separation to lower register footprint
forbidden_patterns: do not mix running-stat updates and heavy activation math in one high-register inner loop
do not assume noncontiguous tensors are safe for vector loads
do not alter GELU semantics without explicit matching

review_notes.openai-compatible: Reasonable tactical improvement for a custom post-op path. Lowering register pressure and separating reduction from apply can make a fused kernel more viable, but the upside is bounded because GEMM remains dominant and vectorization/alignment assumptions may limit applicability. Useful as a supporting optimization, not a primary strategy.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Directly targets the confirmed bottleneck (118 regs/thread, ~33% active warps). Separating reduction state from elementwise apply state and vectorizing the apply pass are correct prescriptions. Gain is modest end-to-end because GEMM dominates, but this makes the custom path viable and avoids the custom kernel being slower than PyTorch primitives â a prerequisite for the other strategies to pay off.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Good incremental tuning advice for the post-op kernel, focusing on register pressure and vectorization.

strategies.intent: Optimize current fused post-GEMM kernel with vectorized loads and stores
strategies.summary: Keep existing architecture (cuBLAS GEMM + custom fused BatchNorm/GELU/ReLU kernel) but optimize the post-GEMM kernel using float4 vectorized memory access, improved warp-level reduction primitives, and tuned block dimensions.
implementation_hints: Replace scalar float loads/stores with vectorized float4 accesses (16-byte aligned)
Current kernel uses 256 threads per feature; experiment with 128 or 512 threads and measure occupancy impact
Use __shfl_xor_sync for warp reductions instead of iterative __shfl_down_sync to reduce instruction count
Unroll the batch-processing loop with #pragma unroll to improve ILP
Consider processing multiple features per block to increase arithmetic intensity
NCU profile shows low long_scoreboard stalls (0.02) and high not_selected stalls (0.34), suggesting warp scheduling inefficiency that better vectorization may address
strategies.expected_gain: 8-15% speedup through improved memory bandwidth utilization and reduced instruction overhead
risk_notes: Vectorization requires alignment guarantees that may not hold for arbitrary batch sizes
Multi-feature-per-block increases shared memory usage and may reduce occupancy
Gains limited since current kernel is already well-optimized (phase-1 attempts show flat speedup)
forbidden_patterns: modifying statistics computation logic
changing kernel launch structure

review_notes.openai-compatible: Incremental but likely low yield. Vectorized loads/stores and tuned reductions can help, yet the proposal explicitly keeps the same architecture that already showed limited gains. Some suggestions also risk alignment and occupancy tradeoffs without addressing the deeper training BatchNorm reduction structure.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Low risk, incremental, and easy to implement alongside other strategies. float4 vectorization, __shfl_xor_sync, and loop unrolling are standard and well-understood. Gains are bounded by how much the post-op kernel contributes to total runtime; the 8â15% claim is plausible at the kernel level but diluted end-to-end given GEMM dominance. Good candidate to apply first as a low-cost baseline improvement.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Vectorizing loads and stores (float4) is a standard and highly effective optimization for memory-bound post-GEMM operations.

strategies.intent: cache and precompute normalization coefficients to shrink non-GEMM overhead, especially in eval mode
strategies.summary: The phase-1 fused post-op produced essentially no runtime change, suggesting fixed overheads and repeated scalar work matter more than raw tensor traffic for the non-GEMM tail. Precomputing per-feature normalization coefficients and reusing extension state can make the post-GEMM path cheaper without changing model I/O.
implementation_hints: For eval mode, precompute per-feature scale and shift derived from running stats, gamma, beta, and epsilon, then let the CUDA path apply them directly before GELU/ReLU.
Cache extension handles, launch configs, and any reusable metadata in helper scope so the forward path avoids repeated setup costs.
If training is active, still precompute invariant affine pointers/metadata and keep running-stat updates isolated from setup-heavy code paths.
Guard the optimized path on contiguous float32 inputs to avoid expensive fallback conversions inside the kernel.
strategies.expected_gain: low to medium; strongest when many repeated forwards reuse the same BN state in eval mode
risk_notes: Cached coefficients must be invalidated when BatchNorm parameters or running stats change.
This is primarily overhead reduction, so gains may be modest for very large GEMMs.
Must not reuse eval coefficients during training.
forbidden_patterns: do not cache training-time statistics across steps
do not hide dtype/layout conversions in the hot path
do not change BatchNorm epsilon or affine ordering

review_notes.openai-compatible: Solid low-risk optimization, especially for eval-heavy reuse. Precomputing per-feature scale/shift and caching reusable dispatch metadata is semantically safe when invalidation is correct, and it avoids repeated scalar/setup overhead. Upside is modest for very large GEMMs, but the implementation risk is comparatively low.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Low risk and easy to implement. Precomputing per-feature scale/shift in eval mode is correct and eliminates repeated scalar arithmetic on the hot path. Gains are modest for large GEMMs but real for repeated inference passes with stable BN state. Most valuable as a complement to strategy_01 rather than a standalone strategy. The main engineering concern is cache invalidation when BN parameters or running stats change.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Caching coefficients might violate benchmark constraints if inputs or weights change across iterations, limiting its applicability.

strategies.intent: Fuse GEMM epilogue into custom kernel to eliminate intermediate writes
strategies.summary: Replace cuBLAS GEMM + separate BatchNorm/GELU/ReLU with a single custom CUDA kernel that performs GEMM with fused epilogue, computing BatchNorm statistics, affine transform, GELU, and ReLU in registers before final writeback.
implementation_hints: Implement tiled GEMM (128x128 or 64x64 output tiles) with warp-level cooperation
Accumulate GEMM result in registers, compute per-feature mean/variance using warp reductions across batch dimension within tile
Apply BatchNorm normalization, GELU approximation (tanh-based), and ReLU in registers before storing to global memory
Use shared memory for input/weight tiles and inter-warp communication for statistics
Handle BatchNorm running statistics update separately if training=True
Profile: NCU shows GEMM kernel is compute-bound (72% SM throughput, 22% DRAM), fusing epilogue eliminates 3 separate memory passes over 16384Ã4096 tensor
strategies.expected_gain: 15-25% speedup by eliminating three 256MB memory roundtrips (BatchNorm, GELU, ReLU reads/writes) and keeping activation data in registers/L1 cache
risk_notes: Complex kernel requiring careful tuning of tile sizes and occupancy
BatchNorm statistics computation must match PyTorch's Welford algorithm exactly
May not outperform cuBLAS if GEMM becomes memory-bound or register pressure limits occupancy
Training mode requires atomic updates to running statistics across tiles
forbidden_patterns: changing BatchNorm axes
altering epsilon value
modifying I/O shapes

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very high risk for this workload. Replacing cuBLAS with a custom fused GEMM+BatchNorm+GELU+ReLU kernel is unlikely to beat vendor GEMM, and exact training BatchNorm statistics/update semantics across a tiled GEMM are complex. Register pressure and occupancy issues are already visible, making this a poor risk-adjusted bet.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Custom GEMM kernels almost never beat cuBLAS/cuBLASLt on Ampere at these tile sizes, and the existing kernel is already at 72% SM throughput. Adding full GEMM logic on top of the already register-pressure-limited post-op path (118 regs/thread) would likely reduce occupancy further and cancel any fusion benefit. The 15â25% end-to-end claim is optimistic; correctness of a Welford-accurate custom BN inside a custom GEMM is non-trivial to verify.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Writing a custom GEMM to fuse the epilogue is extremely risky and likely to underperform highly tuned cuBLAS kernels for large matrices.

strategies.intent: Apply persistent kernel design for BatchNorm statistics aggregation
strategies.summary: Redesign the fused post-GEMM kernel as a persistent kernel where thread blocks cooperatively compute global BatchNorm mean/variance across all features using grid-wide synchronization, then apply affine/GELU/ReLU in a second pass.
implementation_hints: Launch single grid covering all 4096 features with cooperative groups API
First phase: each block computes per-feature mean/variance for its assigned feature subset, stores to global buffer
Grid-wide sync using cooperative_groups::this_grid().sync()
Second phase: blocks read global statistics, apply normalization + affine + GELU + ReLU
Amortizes synchronization cost across large batch (16384 samples)
NCU shows uniform branch behavior (48064 uniform, 0 divergent) and high warp eligibility (56M avg), suggesting good candidate for persistent design
strategies.expected_gain: 10-18% speedup by reducing kernel launch overhead and improving cache locality for statistics buffers
risk_notes: Requires compute capability 6.0+ for cooperative groups grid sync
Two-pass design may increase register pressure and reduce occupancy
Grid sync is expensive; benefits only materialize for large batch sizes
Complex implementation with fragile synchronization semantics
forbidden_patterns: breaking cooperative launch requirements
introducing deadlocks

review_notes.openai-compatible: Poor risk-adjusted choice. Cooperative-grid persistent kernels add significant implementation fragility and portability constraints, while BatchNorm still naturally wants exact global statistics and likely multiple phases. Grid-wide sync overhead and launch restrictions make this unlikely to outperform simpler two-kernel designs.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Persistent kernel with cooperative-groups grid sync is complex and fragile. It increases register pressure (two-pass state), which is already the identified occupancy limiter. The 10â18% speedup estimate assumes synchronization cost dominates, but NCU data does not support that â the bottleneck is occupancy and memory, not kernel launch count. Cooperative launch also restricts maximum grid size and requires explicit SM count management, adding fragility without clear benefit at this problem size.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using cooperative groups for grid-wide synchronization is often slower and more fragile than a simple two-pass kernel design for reductions.

strategies.intent: Pipeline GEMM output chunks with asynchronous BatchNorm/activation processing
strategies.summary: Stream GEMM output in row-chunks, overlapping cuBLAS computation of next chunk with custom kernel processing of current chunk using CUDA streams and async memory operations.
implementation_hints: Split input batch into K chunks (e.g., K=4 for 4096-row chunks)
Create K CUDA streams; launch cuBLAS GEMM for chunk i on stream i, followed by fused BatchNorm/GELU/ReLU kernel on same stream
Use cudaMemcpyAsync or torch::Tensor::split with non_blocking=True to prepare input chunks
Synchronize all streams before final output assembly
BatchNorm statistics require global mean/variance; accumulate per-chunk statistics in shared buffer and compute final values after all chunks complete
NCU shows GEMM kernel at 72% SM utilization; pipelining may hide some of the 22% DRAM latency
strategies.expected_gain: 5-12% speedup if GEMM-to-epilogue latency successfully overlaps with next GEMM computation
risk_notes: Chunking overhead may exceed overlap benefits for this problem size
BatchNorm running statistics update becomes more complex with chunked processing
Stream creation and synchronization overhead may dominate for small chunk counts
Requires careful tuning of chunk size vs. stream overhead tradeoff
forbidden_patterns: changing final output semantics
breaking BatchNorm correctness

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very weak fit because BatchNorm needs global mean/variance over the normalized axis, so chunking the GEMM output conflicts with straightforward fusion/overlap. The extra stream orchestration and chunk assembly add overhead and semantic complexity, with limited chance of meaningful overlap given GEMM is already highly utilized.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Chunked pipelining is fundamentally at odds with BatchNorm correctness: global mean/variance require all samples before the affine pass, so chunk-level BN statistics must be merged before applying normalization, which reintroduces synchronization that likely exceeds the overlap benefit. For a 16384-row batch split into K=4 chunks, stream creation and barrier overhead is non-trivial. The 5â12% estimate assumes ideal overlap that the BN two-pass constraint makes difficult to achieve without a complete redesign of the statistics accumulation.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Chunking the GEMM to overlap with post-ops usually degrades cuBLAS efficiency more than it gains from overlapping.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l2_p41_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION

# <<<IMPROVE:user_helpers>>>
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    """
        Model that performs a GEMM, BatchNorm, GELU, and ReLU in sequence.
        """
    def __init__(self, in_features, out_features):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        self.gemm = nn.Linear(in_features, out_features)
        self.batch_norm = nn.BatchNorm1d(out_features)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, x):
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        # Baseline fallback keeps the official PyTorch forward path.
        # After implementing CUDA_CPP_SRC / CUDA_CU_SRC, call _stark_get_extension().your_entrypoint(...).
        """
                Args:
                    x (torch.Tensor): Input tensor of shape (batch_size, in_features).
                Returns:
                    torch.Tensor: Output tensor of shape (batch_size, out_features).
                """
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        x = self.gemm(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_3>>>
        x = self.batch_norm(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_4>>>
        x = torch.nn.functional.gelu(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_5>>>
        x = torch.relu(x)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_6>>>
        return x
